title: Church and Empire: An 8-Week Study
subtitle: A pastoral, even-handed five-session study on how the church relates to political power, from a denarius in a trap to the end of Christendom, keeping the crucified King above every throne.
summary:
This study is for small groups, adult Sunday school classes, and individuals who feel the ground shifting under the faith in their country and want to know what is actually dying and what is not. It walks slowly through five essays by James Bell on the long marriage of church and empire, from the coin held up to trap Jesus, through the three centuries the church grew with no power at all, to the slow end of the arrangement that made Christianity the default religion of the West. It defines the hard words plainly, never sneers at the believer who grieves the change, and is built to be run by a busy volunteer with zero preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it, every silence has a backup, and every session ends in prayer rather than argument.

This is not a study that flatters the people who want to seize the culture or the people who want to flee it. It catches both. It asks the Christian reaching for the levers of the state whether he has confused a borrowed majority with the work of the Spirit, and it asks the Christian who has washed his hands of public life whether he has called retreat by the name of holiness. Most of all it implicates the leader and the writer. Bell does not stand outside this. He has preached the render line as a permission slip, he has flags on his own platform he has not moved, he grieves the Sunday-closed store he grew up with, and he writes from inside the indictment. So will you.
audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

sessions.title: What Render Unto Caesar Actually Means
sessions.aim: To recover the render line as a fence around a coin rather than a wall between faith and public life, and to ask what we have quietly handed to Caesar that was never his.
sessions.summary: They brought Jesus a coin because they wanted him dead. The Pharisees and the Herodians, who agreed on almost nothing, agreed to set a trap with a single question about a denarius. Pay tax to Caesar, or not. Say yes and lose the crowd that hated Rome. Say no and hand the governor a charge of sedition. We have turned the most dangerous sentence in the Gospels into a permission slip, two tidy drawers, one for politics and one for prayer, and Bell admits he has preached it that way and was wrong. Look at what Jesus does. He asks whose image is on the coin, and the Greek word for image is eikon, the same word Genesis uses when the man is made in the image of God. The coin bears Caesar's image, so give it back. But the thing that bears the image of God is the person holding the coin. Render to God the things that are God's, and the thing that is God's is you. Bell grants the strong version of the comfortable reading first, that the two-drawer instinct kept the church from becoming the state after centuries of religious war, and Caesar really does have a domain. The question is its size. The line does not divide reality in half. It puts a fence around a coin and gives everything else to God. Tertullian saw it. Render the coin to Caesar and yourself to God, for if all things are Caesar's, what will be left for God. They killed him anyway, charged with forbidding tribute and making himself a king. The verse we use to make God small was spoken to make Caesar small.

keyScripture.why: The render line was spoken to spring a trap, and instead of dividing faith from public life it puts a fence around a coin and gives every image-bearer to God.

discussion.q: Before tonight, how had you heard the render line used, and what did it seem to permit?
discussion.behind: Surface the comfortable reading before dismantling it. Most will have heard it as keep your faith out of politics or keep your head down. The point is not to shame the reading but to show the whole room arrived holding the same tidy drawers, so the reversal has somewhere to land. Land it on recognition, not on cleverness.

discussion.q: Bell points out the coin bears Caesar's image but the person holding it bears God's. What changes when you weigh the two drawers instead of assuming they are equal?
discussion.behind: This is the hinge of the whole session. If everything bearing God's image belongs to God, Caesar's drawer holds metal and God's drawer holds every person who ever lived. Help them feel that the line does not split reality in half. It fences a coin and hands the rest to God.

discussion.q: The two-drawer reading protected real things, keeping the church from becoming the state after Europe bled over religion. How do we honor what it got right while seeing what it hid?
discussion.behind: Protect the even-handedness early. The separation instinct is wisdom paid for in blood, not cowardice. You want the room to grant Caesar a real domain before they shrink it, so the conclusion does not sound like the church grabbing for power instead of Rome.

discussion.q: Bell says a church with no power reads the line as a sword and a church with power reads it as a truce, and we have read it as a truce for sixteen centuries. Why would safety change how we hear the same words?
discussion.behind: You want them to see that the words did not change, the reader did. The same sentence that sounded like a sword in the year 64 sounds like a settlement in a comfortable hand. The cost of meaning it is what we lost. Tie this to how easily we domesticate dangerous texts.

discussion.q: Bell ends by asking what we have quietly handed to Caesar that was never his, our final allegiance, our sense of who holds history. What comes to mind when you sit with that question honestly?
discussion.behind: Move from interpretation to self-implication, including the leader. You are not hunting confessions to shame anyone. You want each person to name one place their deepest trust has slid toward a power they can see. Go first if the room is slow.

objections.objection: This is just a way to drag the church into politics. Jesus told us to render to Caesar so we would stay in our lane and keep faith private.
objections.response: Sit with what the lane reading protects before answering. It guarded against the church becoming the state, and that is a real mercy. Then make the distinction gently. Bell is not arguing the church should seize Caesar's throne. He is arguing the line keeps Caesar out of the human soul, not faith out of public life. You can honor that the coin goes back and still refuse to let the emperor have the one thing he most wants, the last word over a creature made in the image of God.

objections.objection: Fine, then everything belongs to God, so a faithful Christian should resist paying taxes and treat the government as Pharaoh.
objections.response: Bell rules this out as plainly as the other error. Jesus did not lead a tax revolt, the coin goes back, and Scripture tells us to honor the emperor in the same breath it tells us to fear God. The render line relativizes Caesar without abolishing him. The point is not to treat every government as an enemy but to refuse the one allegiance that belongs to God alone. Pay the tax. Keep nothing of yourself in his hand.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What is one ordinary loyalty in your life that you have never stopped to ask whether it belongs to Caesar or to God?
sessions.practice: This week, when you pull out a card or a bill to pay for something, let it become a small examination. Ask what else you have been handing over without noticing, your final hope, your sense of who is in charge. Do not fix it. Just notice where your allegiance went and write down what it told you.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, we have used a hard sentence to make ourselves comfortable, and we have handed you the small change while keeping the throne of ourselves. Forgive us for the parts of our hope we have minted in Rome. You stamped your image on us, and we belong to you, not to Caesar, not to a party, not to our own fear dressed up as prudence. Give the coin back to the world this week, and give all of ourselves to you. In the name of the King the empire could not keep buried, amen.
reflection: Where have I read a dangerous text as a domestic one because I no longer stand anywhere it would cost me something to mean it?
What have I quietly placed in Caesar's drawer that bears the image of God and was never his to hold?
If my final allegiance were tested tomorrow, do I actually know where it would land, or have I arranged my life so the trap never springs?

sessions.title: Christendom Is Ending. Christianity Is Not.
sessions.aim: To separate Christendom, the social arrangement, from Christianity, the body of people who confess a crucified Lord, and to grieve the right one.
sessions.summary: A pastor Bell respects told him the country is losing its faith and meant it as a funeral. The polls back him up. Attendance falls, the category of no religion grows fastest, and the assumption that a decent person is probably some kind of Christian has thinned to almost nothing. Bell grieved too, for a while, until he noticed they were grieving two different things and using one word for both. There is Christianity, the people who confess that Jesus is Lord and order their lives around a crucified man who walked out of a tomb. And there is Christendom, the arrangement in which that confession is the default setting of a civilization, baked into its laws and calendar and manners, so that belonging to the culture and belonging to the church feel like the same act. One is dying. The other has survived the death of empires before. Bell carries the mustard seed, the smallest of seeds that becomes a tree, and notes the parable promises growth from smallness, not ownership of the field. He grants the strong defense of Christendom, that it built hospitals and universities and a moral grammar the secular world still borrows without paying, and O'Donovan is right that the gospel genuinely reshaped political authority. But the same arrangement built a Christianity you could inherit without ever meeting Christ, and Kierkegaard called that the great illusion, a nation of Christians none of whom had been confronted by the offense of the cross. The arrangement has a date, 312, the night before the Milvian Bridge, and by 380 Nicene Christianity was the official religion of the state. The end of Christendom is not the defeat of the church. It is the return of the church to the only conditions under which it has ever known how to grow.

keyScripture.why: Jesus describes the kingdom as the smallest of seeds that grows into a tree, promising life from smallness rather than ownership of the field, which Christendom forgot.

discussion.q: Bell says we use one word, Christianity, for two different things, the faith and the cultural arrangement. In your own life, where do you see the two getting confused?
discussion.behind: Open by getting the distinction into the room in plain terms. The faith is people who confess a crucified Lord. Christendom is the setting where that confession is the default. Help them name a place they have treated cultural Christianity and living faith as the same thing, because the rest of the session depends on telling them apart.

discussion.q: The mustard seed parable promises growth from smallness, not ownership of the field. Why did the church spend centuries assuming Jesus meant the empire anyway?
discussion.behind: You want them to feel the gap between what Jesus described and what the church became. He pointed to the smallest thing in the garden. We built the largest thing in the empire and called it the same. Let them sit in how strange that substitution is once you see it.

discussion.q: Bell grants that Christendom built real goods, hospitals, universities, a moral grammar the secular world still borrows. How do we honor those goods while still refusing to grieve the wrong thing?
discussion.behind: Protect the even-handedness. The defenders of Christendom are not cartoon theocrats, they are people who saw what replaces a Christian frame and found it wanting. Make sure no one who grieves the change feels mocked before the harder point lands, that the same arrangement made faith cheap.

discussion.q: Kierkegaard called Christendom a nation of Christians none of whom had met the offense of the cross. Where have you seen faith made cheap simply because it was the default?
discussion.behind: This is the heart of the session. When faith is the default, the word stops meaning anyone in particular. Help them recognize, without contempt, that some of what is falling away now is the nominal and the inherited, an honesty arriving late rather than a pure tragedy.

discussion.q: Bell admits part of him wants the old scaffolding back, the full pews, the easier job, even knowing habit and respectability filled those pews. Where do you feel that same pull?
discussion.behind: Close with self-implication, leader first. The honest confession is that we miss the advantage and call it missing the faith. Invite people to name what they actually grieve, and to ask whether it is Christ or comfort, without rushing anyone to a tidy answer.

objections.objection: This is a convenient way to celebrate the collapse of Christian culture. The decline of faith is a tragedy, and calling it freedom is just spiritualizing defeat.
objections.response: Bell feels the loss honestly and refuses to flatten it. He has five sons inheriting a thinner world, and he says grieve the hospitals if they close and the mercy if it curdles, and fight for those, because they are good. The point is narrower. Cultural Christianity is not the same as the church, and what is dying is partly the nominal and the convenient. You can mourn the real losses without putting the church in the coffin, because the seed is still in the ground.

objections.objection: If Christendom built the hospitals and the universities and the moral grammar, then pulling out the Christian root will rot the fruit, so we should defend the arrangement, not bury it.
objections.response: Grant the strong version fully, because O'Donovan is right that the West was bent by the gospel into new shapes of mercy and law. The question is whether the church protected those goods by being the church or by borrowing the state's machinery. A consensus held by habit is always one generation from collapse. The answer is not to defend the throne but to form a people who would still live the mercy when the culture no longer requires it. That is the church the early centuries actually produced.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: When you picture the faith you want to hand to the next generation, are you picturing a culture that supports it or a community that lives it?
sessions.practice: This week, notice one thing you have always assumed was Christian about your surroundings, a phrase, a holiday, a habit, a closed store. Ask whether it points anyone to the crucified Lord or simply to a culture that used to call itself by his name. Bring what you find back next time.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord of the small seed, we have mistaken the tree we built for the kingdom you planted, and we have grieved the loss of our advantage as though it were the loss of you. Teach us to tell the difference between the church and the culture that wore its clothes. Where cheap faith is falling away, give us the costly kind that has met the offense of the cross. You grew your church under a hostile empire once. Grow it in us again. Amen.
reflection: What am I actually grieving when I grieve the change in my country, the loss of Christ or the loss of an advantage?
Where has the faith been cheap in me because it was the default, never tested against the offense of the cross?
If every cultural support for my faith were gone tomorrow, what of it would still be standing, and what would that tell me?

sessions.title: The Early Church Under Rome: Faith Without Power
sessions.aim: To study the three centuries the church grew with no army, no law, and no protection, and to ask whether we have any idea how to be that church again.
sessions.summary: Pliny the Younger did not know what to do with them, so around the year 112 he wrote the emperor asking how to handle the Christians he kept having to execute, not for any crime he could name but for the obstinacy itself, the flat refusal to do the small civic thing that would have saved them. That is the church we forget. For almost three hundred years, from the cross to Constantine, the faith had no army, no friendly law, no social standing, and no guarantee that confessing the name would not cost a life. And it grew. Bell carries Paul's line written from inside the experience, afflicted but not crushed, perplexed but not driven to despair, and notes the faith lived in that conjunction, in the gap between what the empire could do to the body and what it could not do to the hope. He steel-mans Rome, which was tolerant of religion and read the Christian refusal as sedition dressed as piety, a corrosive sect undermining a fragile civilization. Then he answers. The thing Rome read as corrosion was a different society planted inside the old one, a community that treated a slave and a senator as the same kind of creature, took in the infants Rome left to die, and nursed the sick during plagues when the healthy fled. Stark argued the church grew through plagues precisely because Christians stayed. When you cannot compel, you can only attract. See how they love one another was the only apologetic the empire could see. The blood of the martyrs was the seed, and it was the powerlessness that made the love legible.

keyScripture.why: Paul describes ordinary life under Rome as afflicted but not crushed, naming the gap between what the empire could do to the body and what it could not do to the hope.

discussion.q: Pliny executed Christians not for a crime he could name but for their refusal of one small civic gesture. Why was a pinch of incense worth dying over to them?
discussion.behind: Open on what the empire was actually asking. Rome rarely demanded a change of belief, only a gesture that signaled the state held your final loyalty. The Christians understood the gesture was the whole point. Help the room feel that the martyrs died over the one thing they had already given to Christ, the last word.

discussion.q: Bell points to Paul's grammar, afflicted but not crushed, struck down but not destroyed. What is the difference between not being crushed and winning, and why does it matter that we keep confusing them?
discussion.behind: You want them to separate survival of hope from victory of circumstance. The early church was not winning and was not crushed, and those are different claims. We have spent a long time pretending the second requires the first. Land it on the freedom of a faith that does not need to be winning to be alive.

discussion.q: Rome had real reasons to see the church as antisocial, a sect that would not absorb back into the civic religion. How do we take that seriously instead of treating the persecutors as cartoon villains?
discussion.behind: Protect the even-handedness by honoring the empire's logic. If you believed the gods kept the harvest and the borders, a movement teaching people to insult them looked like a public danger. The point is not that Rome was simply evil but that the church offered a rival society, and that is what scandalized it.

discussion.q: Stark argued the church grew through plagues because Christians stayed and cared for the dying while others fled. What does it tell us that the faith spread fastest exactly when it had the least power?
discussion.behind: This is the reversal. When you cannot compel, you can only attract, and the attraction was bodies that stayed, tables where the wrong people ate together, infants taken in. Help them see that powerlessness made the love legible in a way power later hid. Tie it back to the camouflage of Christendom from session two.

discussion.q: Bell says he fears a future where the faith costs his sons something, but the early church was not afraid the way he is afraid. What are you most afraid of losing, and had the early church already lost it?
discussion.behind: Close with self-implication. The early church had already lost the safety and standing Bell is trying to protect, and found the losing did not touch what mattered. Invite people to name the thing they most fear losing and to ask whether the church Pliny could not explain had it at all.

objections.objection: Romanticizing persecution is easy from a comfortable pew. Suffering is not a strategy, and wishing the church back into the catacombs is a kind of spiritual tourism.
objections.response: Bell guards against exactly this by tracing the cost with dates and blood, Nero after the fire of 64, the martyrs of Lyon in 177, the empire-wide terror under Decius and Diocletian. He does not celebrate suffering. He notices that the church did its clearest work when it had no power, and warns that we should not assume we need the safety we are trying to protect. The point is not to chase martyrdom but to stop believing the faith cannot grow without an advantage it did without for three centuries.

objections.objection: If powerlessness is so holy, then Christians should stay out of public life entirely and let the world run itself while we tend our pure little community.
objections.response: That is the opposite overcorrection, and the early church refutes it. They did not withdraw into a private piety. They built a visible society inside the old one, took in the discarded, stayed through plagues, and confronted the empire's idolatry to its face at the cost of their lives. Faith without power is not the same as faith without engagement. The church that attracts because it cannot compel is more public, not less, lived in the open where the world can see it.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: When have you been drawn to a community not by an argument it made but by the way it treated the people everyone else ignored?
sessions.practice: This week, do one thing the early church was known for that requires no power and no platform. Stay with someone others are avoiding, care for a person the culture has written off, or quietly take responsibility for a need no law requires you to meet. Notice what it asks of you, and whether it feels like loss or like the church remembering its taste.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord, the church you grew had no army and no law and no place to stand, and it outlasted the empire that killed it. We have leaned so hard on safety and standing that we no longer know how to be the church without them. Take our fear of losing what Rome never gave the first Christians. Make our love legible the way theirs was, in bodies that stay when others flee. You had a tomb that would not stay shut. It was enough then. Let it be enough in us. Amen.
reflection: What would my faith look like if it could no longer compel anyone and could only attract, and would there be anything attractive left?
Where am I trusting the safety and standing the early church never had, and calling that trust faithfulness?
What is the small gesture I am unwilling to refuse, the incense I would burn to stay comfortable, and what does that reveal about my final loyalty?

sessions.title: Two Kingdoms: How Christians Relate Faith and State
sessions.aim: To recover the two-kingdoms teaching as a discipline that holds a tension, honoring the office while judging the officeholder, rather than a wall that silences the church or a license that baptizes the state.
sessions.summary: A man asked Bell once whether a Christian should care about politics, and behind the question were two opposite fears, that the church had become a wing of a party, and that answering no would abandon the poor and the unborn and the prisoner. Both fears are right, and the old language of two kingdoms was built to hold them. The phrase means roughly that God rules the world in two ways at once, through the church by the word and the cross, and through the civil order by law and the sword, and that these are not the same rule and must not collapse into each other. It has been abused in both directions, used to tell the church to stay out of public life entirely and used to let the state do whatever it wants. Bell carries the most misused text, let every person be subject to the governing authorities, and shows Paul wrote it to a church the empire would soon burn, not as a blank check but with a leash, since the authority is a servant given a defined job, and a job defined is a job that can be failed. He steel-mans the strongest separation, which is wisdom paid for in blood, the crusade and the inquisition and the wars of religion. Augustine answered from inside the tradition with two cities mingled in history, distinguishable by their loves, telling Christians to seek the city's peace without confusing it with home. The cross is the line. It tells the church it does not rule by force and tells the state it does not rule by right of heaven. The German church learned the cost of forgetting, and Barmen answered that Jesus Christ, not the state, is the one Word we must obey. Two kingdoms, one Lord. Forget the second clause and you have lost the point.

keyScripture.why: Paul commands submission to the authorities and in the same passage defines their job as God's servants for good, so the text that demands submission is the text that lets us judge a state that fails it.

discussion.q: Bell says the man who asked whether Christians should care about politics carried two opposite fears at once. Which of those two fears do you feel more strongly, and why?
discussion.behind: Open by getting both fears into the room, the church as a party wing and the church abandoning the vulnerable. The point is that both are legitimate, and the two-kingdoms teaching exists to hold them together. Notice which fear the room leans toward, because that reveals which abuse it is most likely to commit.

discussion.q: Romans 13 commands submission, but Bell shows the same passage defines the authority's job as a servant for good. How does a job defined become a job that can be failed?
discussion.behind: This is the hinge. The text used to bless tyrants for two thousand years is the same text that puts the state on a leash. If the authority is God's servant with a defined task, the church is exactly the body that can say when the servant has betrayed the master. Help them feel that submission and judgment live in the same verse.

discussion.q: Bell honors the strongest case for keeping the kingdoms separate as wisdom paid for in blood, the crusade, the inquisition, the religious wars. What is that separation rightly guarding against?
discussion.behind: Protect the even-handedness by honoring the separation before complicating it. A church that holds the sword stops persuading and starts coercing, and a state that claims divine sanction becomes a god with an army. Make sure the room sees the separation as hard-won wisdom, not cowardice, before the reversal.

discussion.q: Bell says the German church in the 1930s turned two kingdoms into two sealed rooms, and the sealing let evil rule one room unchallenged. How does the doctrine done right do the opposite of silencing the church?
discussion.behind: This is the reversal, and it is the center of the session. Two kingdoms rightly understood does not free the state from judgment, it subjects the state to a higher court and gives the church a place to stand outside it. Only a church that knows it is a different kingdom can tell Caesar he is not God. Barmen is the model.

discussion.q: Bell confesses he has watched pastors trade the prophetic voice for a seat at the table, whichever party's table, and call it courage. Where have you seen, or felt in yourself, a faith so fused to a program that it could no longer rebuke it?
discussion.behind: Close with self-implication, leader first, and keep it pointed in every direction. The chaplain who cannot rebuke the power he loves comes in a conservative and a progressive version. Invite honest naming of where each person has let a political loyalty silence the word they should have spoken. Go first if needed.

objections.objection: Two kingdoms is just a clever way to tell the church to shut up and stay in its lane while the state does as it pleases. It silences the prophets.
objections.response: That is the abuse Bell names directly, the German error of two sealed rooms, and the doctrine done right reverses it. If the state is God's servant with a defined job, the church is the very body that can say when the servant has failed. The separation is not a wall protecting the state from the church's voice. It is the vantage point from which the church can tell Caesar he is not God. A church that knows it is a different kingdom is the only one that can prophesy to this one.

objections.objection: If the church really believes the gospel, it should pick up the state's power and use it to make the country righteous. Why leave the sword to the unbelievers?
objections.response: Bell rules this out at the cross. The church that grabs the sword forgets its Lord refused it, told Peter to put it away, and conquered by being conquered. A gospel enforced at the point of a sword is no longer the gospel. The two-kingdoms discipline is not passivity. It is serving the city, paying the tax, honoring the office, while keeping one foot in the kingdom of the crucified King, so that when the city asks to be worshiped as a god, the church has somewhere to stand and the words to refuse.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Is there a political power you love so much that you would find it hard to rebuke it even when it was clearly wrong?
sessions.practice: This week, find one place where you have fused the gospel with a political program until you can no longer tell them apart. Practice honoring the office while judging the officeholder, naming one thing your own side has done that the cross condemns. Notice whether you can still see the seam between your faith and your party, and write down what you find.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord, you rule the church by the word and the world by the sword, and you are the one Lord over both. We have collapsed the two into one, sometimes silencing your church to keep the peace, sometimes seizing the state to win. Forgive us for the tables we sold our prophetic voice to sit at. Let us serve the city and pay the tax and honor the office, and keep one foot planted with the crucified King, so that when the city asks us to bow, we have somewhere to stand. Two kingdoms, one Lord. Hold us to the second clause. Amen.
reflection: Which abuse am I more tempted toward, a church that grabs the state's sword or a church that goes silent before it, and why that one?
Where have I so identified the gospel with a political program that I can no longer rebuke the power I love?
Do I honor the office while still judging the officeholder, or have I let my loyalty to a side decide in advance what I am willing to call wrong?

sessions.title: The Church After Cultural Power
sessions.aim: To face that the church no longer sets the terms of the culture and to ask the harder question, whether it ever knew how to be the church without them.
sessions.summary: The store stayed closed on Sunday because the whole town agreed the day belonged to God, and now it does not, and a certain kind of Christian experiences that as the world ending. Bell grew up at the tail end of an arrangement where the culture did half the church's work for free, the calendar and the schools and the social pressure all leaning the way the sermon did. That arrangement is gone, and the real question is not how to get the terms back but whether the church ever knew how to be the church without them. Much of what we mourn as the loss of faith is the loss of advantage. Strip away the home-field edge and attendance falls, partly because the people who never really believed stopped pretending. Bell carries the salt saying, and reads the warning we skip, that salt works by being different from the dish, and the danger is not that the world overpowers it but that it dissolves until no one can taste the difference. He steel-mans the grief, which is love looking at a wound, since real goods eroded when the culture stopped honoring the faith. Then he answers. The church protected those goods by borrowing the state's machinery rather than by being the church, mistaking a borrowed majority for its own strength, learning to win by counting votes instead of making disciples. A victory won that way cannot be kept. The cross exposes what we trusted, because a crucified Lord refutes the idea that the kingdom advances by holding the levers. The end of cultural Christianity is a test of whether anything is left when the advantage is gone, mercy disguised as decline. The culture is done carrying us. Good. Now we find out if we believed any of it.

keyScripture.why: Jesus warns that salt loses its use not when the world overpowers it but when it dissolves until no one can taste the difference, which is what Christendom tempted the church to do.

discussion.q: Bell says much of what we mourn as the loss of faith is really the loss of advantage. Where, honestly, do you feel the difference between grieving Christ and grieving the home-field edge?
discussion.behind: Open on the hardest claim of the session, said gently. The decline is partly a subtraction of the nominal and the convenient, people who never believed no longer pretending. Help the room separate the loss of the faith from the loss of the cultural support, without dismissing the genuine pain in either.

discussion.q: The salt warning is not that the world overpowers the salt but that the salt dissolves until no one can taste it. How was Christendom a long temptation to dissolve?
discussion.behind: You want them to see that the danger was never hostility but sameness. We added ourselves so thoroughly to the culture that no one could taste the difference, voting the same fears, chasing the same security. Tie this back to the camouflage from sessions two and three. Salt does its work by not dissolving.

discussion.q: Bell honors the grief as love looking at a wound, naming real goods that eroded when the culture stopped honoring the faith. How do we take that grief seriously and still ask the harder question?
discussion.behind: Protect the even-handedness. The people mourning lost cultural power are often mourning the unborn, the poor, the support around marriage, real things the gospel cares about. Make sure no one feels their grief is being mocked before the harder point lands, that the goods were held by borrowed power rather than converted hearts.

discussion.q: Bell says the church learned to win by counting votes instead of making disciples, and a victory won that way cannot be kept. Why is a borrowed majority weaker than it looks?
discussion.behind: This is the reversal. A consensus held by cultural habit is always one election from collapse because it rests on power rather than persuaded hearts. The church mistook the home-field edge for its own strength and could not tell how weak it was. Help them feel why formation is slower but sturdier than legislation.

discussion.q: Bell describes two responses to the loss, one fighting to recapture the levers and one quietly building communities so distinct a neighbor has to ask what makes them that way. Which response is more natural to you, and which do you want to hand the next generation?
discussion.behind: Close with self-implication and a real choice, leader first. Bell is not neutral, and neither are you, but invite honesty rather than performance. The first response has a louder voice and a worse record. The second looks like the people Pliny could not explain. Let people name which one they have actually been living.

objections.objection: So the answer is for Christians to retreat into pure little communities and give up on the public square, abandoning the vulnerable to whoever stays in the fight.
objections.response: Bell rules out the retreat as firmly as he rules out the panic. The community he points to is not a bunker, it is a society so distinct that the watching world is drawn to it, the kind that takes in the discarded and forms people who live differently in public. The early church had no cultural power and was not withdrawn, it was the most visible thing in the empire. Losing the levers is not the same as leaving the world. It is finding out whether the church can be salt without the wind at its back.

objections.objection: If Christendom protected the unborn and the poor and marriage, then losing it is a disaster, and the faithful thing is to fight to get the cultural power back.
objections.response: Grant the wound fully, because those goods were real and Bell says fight for them. The question he presses is how the church held them, by being the church or by borrowing the state's machinery of compulsion. A protection that rests on a majority rather than on converted hearts is always one election from collapse, and the church mistook that borrowed strength for its own. The deeper work is forming a people who would live the mercy when the law no longer requires it, which is the only kind of strength the early church ever had.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If the culture stopped doing any of the church's work for you tomorrow, what part of your faith would simply stop, and what would keep going?
sessions.practice: This week, do one thing that makes you distinct rather than blended, one act of mercy or honesty or generosity that the surrounding culture cannot explain and does not reward. Do not announce it. Just notice whether your faith can act on its own, without the wind of approval at its back, and write down what you learn about your own saltiness.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord, the culture is done carrying us, and we are afraid, because we have leaned on it so long we are not sure what is left underneath. Forgive us for trusting the levers more than the cross, for winning by counting votes when you called us to make disciples. Strip away the camouflage. Make us salt that remembers its taste, a people so marked by you that a watching neighbor has to ask what makes us this way. You grew your church with every cultural lever pulling the other way. Do it again in us. Amen.
reflection: How much of my religion is power and advantage, and how much of my witness could survive without the wind at my back?
Have I been fighting to recapture the levers or building a community distinct enough to be noticed, and which one have I called faithfulness?
When the culture stops doing the church's work, what will be left of my faith, and does that answer comfort me or frighten me?

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome. Thank you for being here. Before we start, three things. First, this study was written to indict every tribe, including mine and yours, so we are not here to score points against the people who want to grab the culture or the people who want to flee it. Both are in the room, at least in our hearts. Second, nobody has to perform certainty. You can be unsure out loud, and you can change your mind. Third, the writer puts himself inside everything he says, the render line he preached wrong, the flags he has not moved, the Sunday store he misses, and so will we. We are not pointing from a safe distance. We are standing in it. Tonight we are looking at this theme together: ________. Let me read our key passage, and then we will sit with it before we say anything else. There are no wrong answers in the first five minutes, only honest ones.
facilitatorScript.transition: We have looked hard at what the essay says. Now let us bring it home, off the page and into the week we are about to walk into, because none of this matters if it stays an idea.
facilitatorScript.close: We are going to stop there, even though it is not resolved, because Bell does not resolve it either and neither should we. Take the weight of this out with you rather than setting it down at the door. Try the practice this week. Sit with the reflection questions on your own. And come back ready to be honest, not finished. Let me pray for us before we go, and then I will see you next time. Thank you for the courage it took to be in this conversation.

cadences.name: The full study (8 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Orientation. Read the summary together, set ground rules, and walk session 1's opening questions slowly.
Week 2: Session 1, What Render Unto Caesar Actually Means, full discussion and practice.
Week 3: Session 2, Christendom Is Ending. Christianity Is Not.
Week 4: Session 3, The Early Church Under Rome, part one through Pliny and the grammar of afflicted but not crushed.
Week 5: Session 3 continued, the plagues, the martyrs, and what powerlessness made legible, plus practice.
Week 6: Session 4, Two Kingdoms, the theological center of the study.
Week 7: Session 5, The Church After Cultural Power.
Week 8: Integration. Revisit all five practices, the scripture index, and what each person is carrying out.

cadences.name: The intensive (4 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Sessions 1 and 2 together, the render line and the difference between Christendom and Christianity.
Week 2: Session 3, The Early Church Under Rome, with extended time on faith without power.
Week 3: Session 4, Two Kingdoms, the theological center of the study.
Week 4: Session 5, The Church After Cultural Power, plus a short integration close.

cadences.name: As written (5 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Session 1, What Render Unto Caesar Actually Means.
Week 2: Session 2, Christendom Is Ending. Christianity Is Not.
Week 3: Session 3, The Early Church Under Rome.
Week 4: Session 4, Two Kingdoms, How Christians Relate Faith and State.
Week 5: Session 5, The Church After Cultural Power.

bibliography.title: The City of God Against the Pagans
bibliography.author: Augustine
bibliography.note: The two cities built by two loves, mingled in history until the end, so no earthly nation is the city of God. Written after Rome fell in 410. The deep background for sessions 4 and 5 and the spine of the two-kingdoms tradition.

bibliography.title: The Christians as the Romans Saw Them
bibliography.author: Robert Louis Wilken
bibliography.note: Shows how educated Romans like Celsus and Porphyry read the church as a stubborn, antisocial sect that withheld the small civic gesture holding society together. The fair statement of Rome's case in sessions 1 and 3.

bibliography.title: The Rise of Christianity
bibliography.author: Rodney Stark
bibliography.note: Argues the church grew through plagues because Christians stayed and cared for the dying while others fled, so the math of who survived and who was loved did the rest. The empirical engine of session 3.

bibliography.title: The Ecclesiastical History
bibliography.author: Eusebius
bibliography.note: The early church's own record of the persecutions, including the martyrs of Lyon in 177 in unbearable detail. Grounds the cost of faith without power in session 3 with dates rather than sentiment.

bibliography.title: The Letters of the Younger Pliny
bibliography.author: Pliny the Younger
bibliography.note: The governor's letter to Trajan around 112 asking how to handle the Christians he kept executing for their obstinacy. The primary-source doorway into session 3.

bibliography.title: The Desire of the Nations: Rediscovering the Roots of Political Theology
bibliography.author: Oliver O'Donovan
bibliography.note: Makes the serious case that the gospel genuinely reshaped political authority, that the West was bent by Christianity into new shapes of mercy and law. Used to honor the strong defense of Christendom in sessions 2 and 4.

bibliography.title: Practice in Christianity
bibliography.author: Soren Kierkegaard
bibliography.note: Names the great illusion of Christendom, a nation of Christians none of whom had been confronted by the offense of the cross because everyone was already a Christian by default. Central to session 2.

bibliography.title: Resident Aliens: Life in the Christian Colony
bibliography.author: Stanley Hauerwas and William H. Willimon
bibliography.note: Source of the claim that the church does not have a social strategy, the church is a social strategy, and of the call to read the end of the Constantinian arrangement as opportunity rather than only loss. Anchors sessions 2 and 5. Handle as one strong voice among several, since Bell also affirms public engagement.

bibliography.title: Foolishness to the Greeks: The Gospel and Western Culture
bibliography.author: Lesslie Newbigin
bibliography.note: Written after Newbigin came home to England in 1974 and found a pagan culture with Christian memories. Asks how the gospel addresses a culture that thinks it already knows what the gospel is. Frames the missionary question of session 2. Bell also cites Newbigin's The Gospel in a Pluralist Society on the absence of a neutral public square.

bibliography.title: The Myth of Religious Violence: Secular Ideology and the Roots of Modern Conflict
bibliography.author: William T. Cavanaugh
bibliography.note: Shows how the modern story of secular peace got told, with the state presenting itself as the cool referee that ended religious violence. Complicates the tidy two-drawer reading in session 1. Bell also draws on Cavanaugh's Theopolitical Imagination for the critique of the church as chaplain in session 5.

bibliography.title: To Change the World: The Irony, Tragedy, and Possibility of Christianity in the Late Modern World
bibliography.author: James Davison Hunter
bibliography.note: Documents how thoroughly the church lost its place at the cultural center and how poorly its strategies of political conquest served it. Grounds the diagnosis of session 5.

bibliography.title: Ethics
bibliography.author: Dietrich Bonhoeffer
bibliography.note: Bonhoeffer's break with a two-kingdoms thinking that had decayed into two sealed rooms, written from inside the German church's failure. The conscience behind session 4. Leader to confirm specific chapter references before quoting, since the work is unfinished and compiled.

bibliography.title: The Barmen Declaration
bibliography.author: drafted chiefly by Karl Barth for the Confessing Church
bibliography.note: The 1934 confession that Jesus Christ, not the state, is the one Word of God we must obey, and that there are no areas of life where we belong to another lord. The hinge of session 4. Leader to confirm wording and attribution, often printed in Cochrane's collection of Barth's writings.

furtherReading: Confessions and On Christian Doctrine, Augustine, for the fuller account of disordered love and the use of the earthly city that stands behind the two-kingdoms teaching in session 4.
After Christendom, Stanley Hauerwas, for readers who want to press session 2's claim that the church does not need to run the country, read with the study's affirmation of public engagement in mind.

Defending Constantine, Peter J. Leithart, for a serious counter-voice that resists the simple story that the church was ruined in 312, useful as a steel man against sessions 2 and 5. Leader to confirm.
Theopolitical Imagination, William T. Cavanaugh, for those who want to think harder about the church as its own public rather than a chaplain to the state.
The Rise of Christianity, Rodney Stark, for readers who want the social history behind session 3's claim that the church grew by staying when others fled.

glossary.definition: The line from Mark 12 in which Jesus tells the people to give the coin bearing Caesar's image back to Caesar and to give to God what bears God's image, the human person. Often misread as a wall between faith and public life. It is a fence around a coin.

The long social arrangement in which Christianity was the default setting of a civilization, baked into its laws, calendar, and manners, so that belonging to the culture and belonging to the church felt like the same act. Distinct from the faith itself, which can outlive it.

The pattern, named for the emperor Constantine, of the church aligning with state power after 312 and learning to advance its mission through the machinery of empire rather than through the cross. The founding bargain the study keeps returning to.

The teaching that God rules the world in two distinct ways at once, through the church by the word and the cross and through the civil order by law and the sword, so the two should not be collapsed into one. A discipline that holds a tension, not a wall that silences the church.

The shared beliefs and rituals through which a nation understands itself in relation to the transcendent, with its own sacred objects and holy days. It can humble a nation or flatter it, and it competes quietly with the worship owed to God.

The biblical condition of God's people living as a minority under a power not their own, told to seek the welfare of the city while never mistaking it for home. The posture the early church knew and the post-Christendom church is relearning.

Paul's language for the structures, authorities, and spiritual forces that order the world and can become idols when they demand the allegiance owed to God alone. The empire, the state, and the culture can each become one.

Augustine's image of the earthly city built by love of self and the city of God built by love of God, mingled together in this age so that no nation is wholly either one, distinguishable by their loves rather than their borders.

glossary.term: Salt that has lost its taste
glossary.definition: Jesus' warning in Matthew 5 that salt is useless once it dissolves into the dish and can no longer be distinguished from it. The image for a church so blended into its culture that it can bear witness to nothing beyond it.

Jesus' picture of the kingdom as the smallest of seeds that grows into a tree, promising life from smallness rather than ownership of the field. The corrective to a faith that mistook itself for the empire.

The movement within the German church in the 1930s that refused to fuse the gospel with the state, declaring at Barmen that Jesus Christ alone is the one Word of God to be obeyed. The case study of two kingdoms done right under pressure.

The witness of those who would not perform the small public gesture that signaled the state held their final loyalty, and died rather than give Caesar the last word that belonged to Christ. The blood that, Tertullian said, became the seed of the church.

Treating something other than God as ultimate. The idol is rarely a bad thing, it is usually a good thing, a country or a culture or a coin, asked to be God, which is exactly how an empire becomes one.
The biblical claim that the human person bears God's likeness, the eikon, so that every person belongs to God in a way no coin or empire ever can. The hidden answer Jesus gives in the render trap.

promoKit.bulletinBlurb: From a coin held up to trap Jesus to the slow end of the arrangement that made Christianity the default religion of the West, the church has always had to figure out how to live under power it does not hold. This five-session study walks slowly through what we owe Caesar and what we owe God, the three centuries the church grew with no power at all, and what is actually dying as the culture stops carrying us. It is even-handed, indicting both the grab for the levers and the retreat from public life, and it is built so any volunteer can lead it with no prep. Join us as we keep the crucified King above every throne.
promoKit.pulpitAnnouncement: We are starting a five-week study called Church and Empire, and before anyone braces for a political fight, hear this. It is not a campaign for a party, and it is not a call to abandon the public square. It catches the Christian who wants to seize the culture and the Christian who wants to flee it, and it implicates all of us. It asks a simple, hard question, what do we owe Caesar, and what belongs only to God. No homework, no prep needed to lead a group. Sign up at the welcome table.
promoKit.inviteCaption: Give the coin back to Caesar. Keep nothing of yourself in his hand. A five-session study on how the church has lived under empire from Rome to right now, even-handed about both grabbing power and fleeing it, and built so anyone can lead it. Come honest, not finished.
